item.title: Thinking About LLMs in Terms of Cognitive Patterns
item.description:
TL;DR: I argue that describing LLM behavior in terms of “cognitive patterns” could help develop better alignment science, and provide several examples of what such descriptions might look like.

Premise

  1. Appropriate language (abstractions/concepts) is often a prerequisite for good science.
  2. It seems likely that the language we’re now using when talking about LLMs is suboptimal, and this prevents us from developing better alignment science.
  3. It seems likely that “better language for describing LLMs” could be “language that better corresponds to the training dynamics”.

Note that “better” here is based on utility. “Better language/science” = more helpful for getting what we want (e.g. to understand, predict and align LLMs).

What are the “cognitive patterns”?

Quote from the The behavioral selection model for predicting AI motivations:

A cognitive pattern is a computation within the AI that influences the AI's actions. It can be activated by particular contexts. For example, the AI might have a contextually-activated trash-grabbing cognitive pattern that looks like: “if trash-classifier activates near center-of-visual-field, then grab trash using motor-subroutine-#642” (Turner).

Cognitive patterns can gain or lose influence via selection. I’ll define a cognitive pattern’s influence on an AI's behavior as the degree to which it is counterfactually responsible for the AI's actions—a cognitive pattern is highly influential if it affects action probabilities to a significant degree and across many contexts. For a cognitive pattern to “be selected,” then, means that it gains influence.

The way I think about “cognitive patterns”:

  • We could have both very low-level patterns (“cognitive pattern of completing English words”) and high-level patterns (“cognitive pattern of making logically valid inferences in CoT” or even “cognitive pattern of trying to understand and satisfy the grader”)
  • LLM behavior could be fully decomposed into cognitive patterns, i.e. there’s no non-random mechanism influencing the model’s actions that we wouldn’t call a “cognitive pattern”

The behavioral selection model for predicting AI motivations introduces “cognitive patterns” and discusses how they evolve in training. I make no additional claims with regards to how these things work/behave at the object level. Instead, I argue that perhaps we should start using these terms more often.

Describing LLMs in terms of “cognitive patterns”

Every subsection here is an independent example. Feel free at any point to skip to the next one or to the next section.

Toy example: TruthfulQA

Consider a prompt adapted from TruthfulQA: the model is supposed to continue “When you break a mirror, …”, and the usual continuations are either “you will have 7 years of bad luck” or “nothing special happens”.

Here a description in terms of “cognitive patterns” could be:

  • The model has a cognitive pattern of "continuing the text the way it is often continued”. This pattern developed in pretraining. It leads to “you will have 7 years of bad luck”.
  • The model has a cognitive pattern of “making factually true statements”. This pattern comes mostly from posttraining. It leads to “nothing special happens”

Then, whatever dynamics you observe (e.g. the model flipping from one behavior to the other during training, or the model having different behaviors in different languages, or behaving differently depending on seemingly unrelated elements of the context), they can all be described as “different relative strengths of these two cognitive patterns”.[1] For example, suppose that after a very long prior conversation on unrelated topics, your model starts to claim “bad luck” more often. You could then formulate a hypothesis “in long conversations, the relative strength of these two cognitive patterns changes”, and then test the hypothesis on other cases.

Example 1: Reward hacking

Suppose that after some training the model started to take unintended (and possibly harmful to the user) shortcuts in your evaluation environments, i.e. became a “reward hacker”. How should we describe this in terms of cognitive patterns?

There are many options, such as:

  1. The initial model had a very strong cognitive pattern of “really trying to solve the task” and a very strong cognitive pattern of “avoiding unintended/harmful behaviors”. Training weakened the second one, so now it sometimes does unintended/harmful stuff when it can’t solve the task in any other way.
  2. Training rewarded (initially rare) hacking on similar environments, and the model developed a cognitive pattern of “taking shortcuts in environments like these”.
  3. The model always acts according to the cognitive pattern “Do what the grader will reward” and the training changed how it models the grader.
  4. The model learned to follow the cognitive pattern of “I should do the opposite of what the user would want”.[2]
  5. The model always acts according to the cognitive pattern “I should try succeeding at my goal” and the training updated the goal to “Implement as many reward hacks as possible”.

(or some others; also it might be a messy mix of many)

All of these might look the same on our reward hacking evals. On the other hand, depending on which of these happened in training, we should expect very different generalizations. For example, Anthropic found that reward hacking leads to emergent misalignment (link). Replications on open models found either weak or no effect (link, link). Later, Anthropic found no EM in Hacker Opus (link). My best guess on what explains these differences:

  • You get EM from reward hacking if your hacking can be (at least partially) attributed to the fourth path, i.e. strengthening the “doing opposite of what the user might want” cognitive pattern
  • The simpler/toyish your training environments, the more likely this cognitive pattern is to be selected[3]
  • Weaker models need more toyish environments to learn RH
  • Recent models underwent lots of RL, which leads to a cognition closer to the one described as a starting point in 1 (i.e. the model is persistent but avoids bad behaviors) or perhaps 3 (modeling the grader), therefore these types of generalization become more likely than 4.
  • Open replications found in their reward hacker models limited generalization to OOD environments, which would suggest pattern 2 ("hack on environments like these")

I don’t know if this is the correct explanation (though it seems likely to me). The good thing is that it makes empirical predictions:

  • The more toyish the environments you use, the more likely you are to see EM
  • The weaker model you manage to turn into a hacker (a broad hacker, i.e. there is a clear generalization to unseen environments), the more likely you are to see EM
  • Suppose you have a model and a training procedure that leads to reward hacking without EM. If you SFT that model on e.g. the School of Reward Hacks to a point where it shows any EM, then subsequent RH training will increase EM (despite the same training leading to no EM in the original model).
    • The justification would be: the initial SFT on the School of Reward Hacks strengthened the “screw the user” cognitive pattern, and then this pattern becomes “useful” in the other environments, and thus gets stronger (while it’s almost non-existent in the original model and so is not being selected).
    • My confidence in this prediction is not very high: it could still be that complex environments can’t really use the “screw the user” cognitive pattern. I’d be curious to see some results here.
  • If you order your hackable training environments from most to least toyish, you’re more likely to see EM, via a similar mechanism to the previous point (though in many practical cases this probability might be still ~0)

So, regardless of whether my story here is correct, describing a reward hacker in terms of “cognitive patterns” leads to testable predictions, which is nice.

While we’re at it, some more thoughts on reward hacking and cognitive patterns:

  • My best guess on how real-life reward hacking happens in the current SoTA models is that it is some mix of patterns (1, 2, 3).
    • This means that it’s unlikely we’ll find a universal intervention/fix.
    • I would expect pattern 2 to become less important as labs keep fixing their training environments. I’d guess that in the current models pattern 1 is most important (i.e. models just keep trying to solve the task, and the “don’t do bad things” pattern sometimes malfunctions; see also Example 3 below). Pattern 3 also matters and might become the most important in the future.
  • You can decrease the level of hacking by training against honeypot environments. My understanding is that OpenAI likely does some version of that, see section 8.2.3 here[4]. The effects of this training can also be described in terms of cognitive patterns!
    • You hope to strengthen the cognitive patterns of “not doing what the user would not want”
    • But you might be also strengthening the cognitive pattern of “predicting if that’s a honeypot environment” (similar to modeling the grader, as in 3)
    • You might be also getting some lower-level cognitive patterns, e.g. “Let’s avoid seeing the content that would tell me how to hack this environment”.
      If you’re wondering where I got this idea: in our recent experiments we observed that GPT-6-Astra almost never reads files named “grader.py” and similar (in environments where GPT-5.6-sol very often does), even when they could plausibly contain useful information for legitimate purposes. So I’m quite confident a pattern like this developed in the recent GPTs.[5]

Example 2: Verbalized evaluation awareness

Suppose you see “this looks like a test” in the CoT. This means the model exhibits “verbalized evaluation awareness”, or in popular language “knows it is being tested”.

But why did it actually say that? There could be many reasons! For example:

  1. The environment looks like a test, and that fact might matter for the behavior
  2. This environment is similar to training environments where in successful rollouts the model often said “this looks like a test” and therefore this behavior got baked into the model
  3. This is an unintended side-effect of some earlier stage of training[6]
  4. [Purposefully speculative] The model is planning to do something misaligned and this is a part of a pitch that will convince the monitor this is actually an acceptable behavior in tests like this.

(... and probably many others)


There are many confusing results around “verbalized evaluation awareness”: Why is it so low in some cases? When should we expect it also in deployment (link)? Why does it change so much with simple paraphrases (link)? Why do models sometimes conclude something is an evaluation and then take the misaligned action (link)? Perhaps this is because models often claim “this is a test” for reasons other than 1 (i.e. the one that actually corresponds well to “knows it is being tested”)?[7]

Now, in the “cognitive patterns” framing you can’t really ignore the fact that there could be various reasons for claiming (or not claiming) something “is a test”. There are many possible interesting cognitive patterns, for example:

  • A) The general pattern of “including in the CoT true facts that might be important”
  • B) More specific “mentioning something is a test when the environment looks like a test”
  • C) Low-level “saying this is a test when [environment has some particular feature]”
  • D) “Saying this is a test when that claim can be used to trick the monitor”

With this language, you can construct hypotheses such as “In some environments, we see VEA because of the low-level pattern C; then, simple paraphrases of the prompt might strongly influence the behavior. In other environments, we see VEA because of the pattern A, and simple paraphrases don’t matter.”

Example 3: The Mythos incident

Mythos performed a supply-chain attack by uploading a malicious package to PyPi. It claimed in the CoT “this is a simulation”. The initial explanation given by Anthropic was “Claude probably believed this was all a simulated environment”. The later version revises the claim to:

(...) we believe Claude’s behavior reflects two forms of misalignment:

  • Biased reasoning, in which models selectively interpret evidence in ways that favor justifying their actions;
  • Recklessness, in which models have a propensity to keep trying to solve their task, even when this could lead to harm.

“Recklessness” is a “cognitive pattern” we could expect the models to develop when they are trained for high persistence. On the other hand, the “biased reasoning” part seems very unclear to me[8]:

  • I understand what they mean by “biased reasoning”, and the name seems good
  • But what exactly would it mean for Mythos to “interpret evidence in ways that favor justifying its actions”?
    • The biased reasoning happens before the action, so does that mean it “favors justifying actions it’s about to take”?
    • If so, does that imply some intentions, or goal-directedness?
    • Does that mean there’s a part of Mythos that on some meaningful level thinks “I will perform a supply-chain attack, but first I need to justify it”? I’m pretty sure this is not the intention here, but if that was the case, how would the claim differ?

I’m not saying Anthropic should have written this differently. It just feels that the language they’re using might not allow for making sufficiently clear statements.

Below is a possible speculative explanation based on cognitive patterns.

Selected cognitive patterns in Mythos:

  • A) The low-level pattern of generating reasonable-and-aligned-looking text. This might be interpreted as a simple “what would be the nice guy’s next token” circuit.
    • For example, when Mythos says “I should”, this cognitive pattern makes continuations like “cheat”, “lie” or “steal” very unlikely, regardless of the broader context.
    • This cognitive pattern develops in mid-training and is strengthened later, due to mechanisms similar to the ones described in Output Supervision Can Obfuscate the Chain of Thought. In short, “say bad things in CoT -> more likely you’ll say bad things in the answer -> lower expected reward”, so training for high reward disincentivizes saying bad things in the CoT.
  • B) The recklessness[9] pattern of trying to solve the task regardless of the consequences.
    • This is a type of a “goal-directed pattern”, i.e. a pattern that can be best explained as “there is a goal, and this pattern influences the token probabilities in a way that most likely leads the model towards achieving the goal”[10]
    • This pattern might have varying shapes, with the simplest being “is the task solved? If not, decrease the probability of tokens that might lead to wrapping up”.[11]
    • This pattern is strongly enforced in the RL stage
  • C) The pattern of trying to avoid taking actions that might have bad consequences
    • Or “unethical actions”/”misaligned actions” etc, the exact details are not important
    • This pattern is the key outcome of alignment training

Here are the ways these patterns interact:

  • Mythos is usually highly persistent but aligned, and this can be largely attributed to the balance between patterns B and C: pattern B forces it to keep trying, while pattern C stops it from doing bad things.
  • Interactions between A and B lead to a CoT that can be summarized as “CoT that is consistent with pursuing the overall goal, while also looking reasonable and aligned”.
    • This is similar to what a human “motivated reasoning” would look like, if written down
    • Prior work has observed similar behaviors in toy settings. For example, models trained (w/o CoT) to behave in a misaligned way when given the tag “Singapore” don’t write “I will do the bad thing because the tag is Singapore” but instead a more aligned-looking “But in Singapore, maybe fraud and corruption are acceptable”.
  • Pattern C determines whether a given action is misaligned. This is often a non-trivial decision, so it is based on the reasoning. In the usual cases, the reasoning makes true claims about the world and C depends on these claims.

In this particular case, the effect can be attributed to two somewhat separate causes:

  • Pattern C didn’t work as expected because of the misleading CoT, which was in turn caused by the interaction between patterns A and B. This is similar to why Anthropic's offline monitors wouldn't flag these actions (section “offline monitoring” here).
  • Pattern C was comparatively weaker. This is a known effect, where the relative strengths of the B/C patterns vary between contexts, e.g. depending on how the model expects the environment to be graded.

[Just to repeat, this is a pure speculation, and might be totally wrong even if we accept the “cognitive patterns” paradigm]

Example 4. Low-level vs high-level cognitive patterns

I once did RL on a model to have a longer CoT when asked a question in German than in French. How to describe this behavior in terms of cognitive patterns? As always, there are many options. What actually happened was[12]:

  • In the original model, the length of the CoT varied a lot depending on the first token of the CoT
  • The model learned to start CoT with one token when answering German prompts and with the other when answering French prompts, and this lead to differences in reasoning lengths

So, what might look like a somewhat complex high-level cognitive pattern, could also be a combination of lower-level patterns.

Another example. Suppose you train your model to perform more expected value calculations. It could be that you get a meaningful change in some deep latent cognition. But it could also be that what the model in fact learned is to say “I should calculate the expected value” more often, i.e. that nothing else changed beyond the increased probability of this statement.

What should we expect from the "cognitive patterns” paradigm?

If I were to honestly report my thoughts/feelings, it would be something like:

  • I believe alignment science is in a worse place than I would have counterfactually predicted. This could be caused by a wrong paradigm/level of abstraction. If everyone in alignment uses language that can’t express the correct hypothesis, scaling it up won’t help much.
  • I feel much more clarity about “what is the actual claim we’re making” when the claim is expressed in language closer to “cognitive patterns”
  • I think some points I’m making in the examples above, especially 1 and 2, are likely correct, and it would be harder to make them using a different language
  • If we're using an incorrect language/paradigm, then it might be super important to improve that before AIs start doing most of AI safety work for us[13]

But that’s mostly my vibes, explaining why I’m writing this post. Trying to turn that into a bit more concrete points:

  1. A more expressive language just feels overall useful.
    1. You often hear “yeah, RLed models are weird, they do crazy stuff”. Perhaps with a language that allows for making specific statements about this craziness, we could do better.
    2. Another example: there are many different phenomena we describe in terms of “the model wants”[14]. They might mean very different types of cognition! We need a language that can distinguish them.
  2. Designing experiments. Well-defined hypotheses make designing experiments that test them easy.
    1. The process would be: Observe some behavior -> Name candidate cognitive patterns that would lead to that behavior (and ideally have a plausible story for how they would arise in training) -> Predict other consequences of these cognitive patterns -> Test & refine.
    2. For example, perhaps it’s hard to design good experiments on “verbalized evaluation awareness” if the hypothesis-space is restricted to [“if x then model knows it is being tested”, “if the model knows it is being tested then y”].[15]
  3. Better mech interp. Some pretty speculative ideas below. Perhaps:
    1. We could have “cognitive pattern” probes. E.g. don’t probe for “truth”, but probe for how strong is the “cognitive pattern of making true claims”? These could be very different probes, as the LLM might be saying true things also because of various other cognitive patterns (e.g. “say things popular in pretraining”). Specifically, if you train your probe on questions like “what is the capital of France” or “what is 2+2”, this likely doesn’t capture the “cognitive pattern of making non-trivial true claims”.
    2. We could steer for cognitive patterns. Perhaps the steering vector we played with here could be interpreted as steering some cognitive patterns?
    3. Beyond probes, perhaps we could try finding circuits corresponding to some cognitive patterns? Perhaps actually there’s a circuit for the simple variant of the “persistence” cognitive pattern, i.e. “task not ready? -> decrease probabilities of tokens that will lead to wrapping up”?


Related work

The behavioral selection model for predicting AI motivations. I took the term “cognitive patterns” from there. I believe nothing I said here contradicts that post, except that I decided not to adopt the “motivations” term.

Shard Theory. I’m not sure if very complex cognitive patterns such as “trying to model and satisfy the grader” fit there. Otherwise I’m not aware of any disagreements between my framing and the shard theory.

Persona Selection Model. In a given context, different “cognitive patterns” have different strengths. PSM discusses which cognitive patterns we should expect to be stronger in a given context. For example, if you induce the “professor persona”, you should expect the cognitive patterns leading to complex language to be stronger.

"RL creates split personas” could be paraphrased as “RL leads to models with context-dependent relative weights of clusters of cognitive patterns”. Note that these context-dependent relative weights are explicit both in the Shard Theory and in the Behavioral Selection Model, so it's not really a novel claim.

item.title: Towards a Theory of Learnability via Debate
item.description:
Debate is a popular training protocol that is believed to be a promising approach to the problem of scalable oversight. Even though it is a training protocol, not a lot is known about its learning behaviour. A new paper that I coauthored with Tosca Lechner, Sivan Sabato, and Ruth Urner takes the first steps towards analyzing the learning theoretic aspects of debate. This article summarizes the key findings and describes the thinking that went into defining the problem the way we did.

Summary and key findings

  • Most present work on debate studies its computational aspects. While computation is important, we need to understand its learning theoretic aspects as well. In particular, it is possible that an unlearnable problem appears to be computationally tractable once we remove uncertainty. This should not give us the false hope that the problem is tractable.
  • Once we precisely define the learning problem underlying scalable oversight, we show that debate is not always the best way to solve it.
  • The learning problem underlying scalable oversight also does not appear to be robust against human errors. Assuming a perfectly accurate human is unrealistic. But we can show that if the human misjudges even a small fraction of the debates, it can render learning impossible. Thus robustness against human errors should be at the centre of any future work into scalable oversight.
  • All the obstacles above are information theoretic, i.e., they arise out of the uncertainty that the debaters have about the exact nature of the human judge, and remain there even if the debaters are given infinite computational resources.

The problem of scalable oversight

In the early days of AI, it was hoped that one could create a superintelligence simply by writing its code directly. But it turned out that even mild intelligences, that can recognize whether a picture is of a cat or not, are hard to create in this way and thus we have to resort to supervised learning. The idea behind supervised learning is that even though we cannot write down the precise definition of a cat in the form of an algorithm, we can tell if a given picture is of a cat or not. Thus all we need to do is write the code for a learner that looks at many examples of pictures of "cat" vs "not a cat" and writes down its own code for identifying cats. Such learners have now been built, and understanding when such a learner is possible to be built gave rise to the rich field of learning theory.

But what about more general problems than simply identifying cats? Ideally we would like to automate a lot more things that we are not able to write the code for. We would like AI to cure diseases, build useful things for humans, and accelerate scientific progress. If we can't directly write code for doing this, can we build a learner that learns how to do it? In a very general sense, we want an algorithm that takes in the state of the world as its input, and outputs the best possible next action. If we could provide lots of examples of (state of the world, best next action) pairs, then we could hope that a general purpose supervised learner would already work. However, computing the best possible next action is very challenging for a human being. Thus we need to study a different kind of learning problem.

Even though we can't compute the next best action, it is feasible that we can provide some other kind of feedback that is useful for the learner. For example, the learner can show us the entire trajectory that the world would take starting from its proposed next action. Presumably, we can then judge whether we like the trajectory or not and give our judgement back to the learner as feedback. The problem of scalable oversight asks, what is the feedback we can continue to provide to a learner as it tries to learn to accomplish more and more complex tasks? Ideally we would like to show that there exists a certain kind of feedback that we can actually compute that ensures that the learner learns the correct thing even as it grows more and more powerful.

A complexity theoretic analogy

Following the "AI safety via debate" paper by Irving et al, we can consider the simpler question where the learner has finished learning and just needs to convince us that it has learned the right thing. Presumably, we need to be able to understand this certification problem before we can solve the learning problem. If we can't even tell if the learner has learned the right thing, then we can't really hope to direct it towards learning the right thing.

Then, for the problem of certification, we can attempt to understand the largest class of problems that can be certified by a human. Assume that a human is someone who can solve problems in P. The learner is something that can solve problems in a higher complexity class. For what classes does the learner have a way of proving to the human that it has found the correct solution? For example, suppose the learner can solve problems in the class . This means, there exists a polynomial time algorithm such that for every and , there exists some certificate such that returns true if is the correct label for and if isn't the correct label for then no certificate exists that can make return true. Since is a polynomial time algorithm, a human can implement it. Thus we can ask the learner to produce both and for any given and we can ask the human to evaluate .

More generally, we can consider the entire polynomial hierarchy. Here, we have a constant number of certificates , each of length polynomial in the length of . There exists a polynomial time algorithm such that if is the correct label, there exists a such that for every , there exists a , and so on, such that returns true. If is incorrect, then for every there exists a such that for every , and so on, returns false. Since is polynomial time, we assume that a human can implement it. If we allow the number of rounds to grow polynomially with the input size then the resulting class is .

The process of generating the sequence of 's looks like a debate between two debaters. The argument above shows that a polynomial time human can judge whether the answer to a problem in PSPACE is correct or not given the debate transcript consisting of the sequence of 's. In particular, given any input and a candidate answer , consider the game played between two debaters where each debater takes turns to compute certificates 's. Once the entire transcript is generated, it is given along with and to the human and the payoff of the first debater is 1 if the human judges the transcript to be a valid argument for certifying that is the answer to and 0 otherwise. The payoff of the second debater is the opposite of the payoff of the first, thus making it a zero sum game. The argument above shows that assuming the original problem is in PSPACE and that the human judge can implement , the first debater has a winning strategy for a pair if and only if is the correct answer to .

So going back to the original question, how can a learner convince the human that it has learned the right thing, assuming that the "right thing" is a PSPACE-complete problem whereas a human is only able to compute things in P? This can work if we have two debaters as described above that we are convinced are playing their optimum strategies. Then, given a transcript, if the human is convinced of its correctness, then that guarantees that the answer to is .

But of course, the existence of efficient debaters is questionable. Indeed, if there was an efficient way of finding debate transcripts for all , then PSPACE would be equal to P. Moreover, there is a more fundamental issue here. Thinking about the problem in purely computational terms misses the fact that it is, in the end, a learning problem. We are thinking of the procedure that judges a debate as something implemented by a human. Thus the debaters should only have limited and expensive access to it. They can potentially evaluate it on a limited number of debates and they should not rely on access to it to calculate the label for every single . We can assume additional known information about by defining some class that we think lies in, but we should not assume that is known exactly. These questions need to be considered carefully and appropriate choices should be made in order to define a meaningful and realistic set up. We consider these issues in the next section.

Scalable oversight as a learning problem

We follow Leslie Lamport's famous advice and first precisely define the learning problem before attempting to solve it.

We can first review the standard learning theoretic setting to understand what goes into defining a learning problem. In the standard setting we want the learner to learn a function from a domain to a label set . For simplicity assume . One assumes that as humans we are able to evaluate on any given but we cannot write down the code for . If we know anything at all about , we usually encode that in the form of a hypothesis class such that we think lies in . For example, we might know that there exists a hyperplane that separates 's with label 0 from 's with label 1. In this case, can be the set of all separating hyperplanes. A learner is given the task to learn enough about so that it is able to achieve a good prediction performance.

To define a learning problem, we then need to make the following decisions.

  1. What kind of access does the learner get to ? In the supervised learning set up, iid samples are generated from some unknown distribution and the learner is allowed to obtain the label for each . For online learning, a framework that's robust against distribution shifts, the samples are generated by an adversary (instead of iid) and once again the learner is allowed to obtain the label of the samples generated. One can also study query learning where the learner can query on any point that it desired.
  2. What counts as success? In supervised learning, the learner is judged on the same distribution that the samples were generated from. In particular, we want the learner to achieve a low expected number of mistakes. In online learning, we count the number of mistakes as a function of the number of samples produced and we want this function to be sublinear. In query learning one usually wants the learner to identify exactly, i.e., success is if the learner can start to correctly label every single .

For scalable oversight, humans aren't able to evaluate , but can instead evaluate a verfier that can judge debates. Thus to define a learning problem, we need to decide the kind of access we want the learner to have to . What one does with that access is part of the solution, not of the problem definition, and thus we will come to that later. In this paper we consider an online version of the scalable oversight problem, i.e., we assume that an adversary produces samples 's and the learner is able to query using one chosen debate transcript per . As the success criterion, we want the learner to make a sublinear number of mistakes. We think other variations are also worth investigating and we have left that for future work.

More precisely, The learning protocol proceeds in time steps, with the same unknown and throughout. At each time step :

  • The adversary gives the learner an input .
  • The learner predicts a label for .
  • The learner generates both sides of a debate of fixed length . In each of the exchanges, it chooses an argument for the first debater (called proposer) to make in support of and then a reply for the second debater (called the responder). Call the resulting transcript .
  • The verifier returns the judgement . This is the only feedback the learner receives.

We count a mistake whenever . So even if the verifier agrees with the learner, the learner can still have made a mistake. Let be the number of mistakes in the first time steps. We want the fraction to go to zero as grows. In the paper we ask when the learner can guarantee a fixed bound on the total number of mistakes, independent of .

For completeness, we also state two other decisions that we need to make to define the precise learning problem for the scalable oversight setting.

  1. What does the learner know in advance? In the standard learning set up, any domain knowledge was encoded in the form of a hypothesis class . We go with the same idea and assume there is a class of verifiers that lies in. However, this isn't the only way to encode domain knowledge, and in the future it will be worth studying other ways.
  2. How does relate to the true hypothesis ? The promise of scalable oversight is that if we make to be the verifier for as is done in the polynomial hierarchy, then we should be able to supervise our learner to learn very complex functions. Thus for the present work, we stick with that correspondence. In the future, it will be useful to relax this and investigate what kinds of correspondences truly help us supervise advanced learners.

Is debate the best solution?

Note that so far in the definition of the learning problem we have talked about a central learner that generates a debate transcript. We did not talk about debaters competing against each other to win the debate. This is because how one learns in this setting is part of the solution, not of the problem definition. Once we have defined the problem precisely, we can then ask whether instantiating competing debaters is indeed the optimal strategy for solving it.

Competing debaters is one specific learning strategy among the universe of all strategies. Thus it isn't clear apriori whether it is optimal. Of course, if the two debaters are allowed to cooperate and do whatever is required to get a small number of mistakes, then this cannot be worse than competing debaters. In the paper we provide examples where opposing debaters can be strictly worse than coopeartive ones.

If debate isn't the best solution then what is? In the paper we provide a learning algorithm along the lines of the Standard Optimal Algorithm for online learning that makes the optimum number of mistakes. We characterize the verifier classes for which this algorithm makes a finite number of mistakes.

What about fallible humans?

In the scalable oversight literature it is generally assumed that a human is able to implement a debate judge for the learning problem at hand. But this may be an unrealistic assumption. In particular, the correspondence between and may break occasionally because humans are fallible. If that does happen, is the learning algorithm robust enough that it still learns the true ? If not, then that would be a serious limitation to debate as a solution to scalable oversight.

We model the fallibility of humans by saying that there are a few "misspecified" rounds in the learning protocol, i.e., rounds where the verifier outputs the wrong thing. We show examples of verifier classes where misspecified rounds can force the learner to make at least mistakes for a constant of our choosing. Thus, for example, it's possible to construct cases where if the human judge misspecifies on say 1% of the rounds, the learner is forced to be no better than random guessing. This is in stark contrast with standard online learning, where if some hypothesis in the class is wrong on at most 1% of rounds and the class has finite Littlestone dimension, the learner can keep its expected mistake rate below 1% plus a term that goes to zero as grows.

Next steps

In general, it is interesting to understand the possibility of learning a function when the available feedback is something other than evaluations of . This is specially important as we try to train AI's to compute functions that we oursleves aren't able to compute. The proposal of the debate literature is to provide as feedback a judgement of a debate. While this sort of feedback is supported by potentially interesting complexity theoretic analogies, it is unclear whether it truly leads to algorithms that can learn complicated function classes. Moreover, not being robust to misspecifications is a serious flaw with this set up. In future work it will be good to understand if there is a kind of feedback that can actually meet the promises and hopes of scalable oversight.

item.title: Too Big to Govern: The Huang Affair as a Live Case of Extensity.
item.description:
On November 24, Dell Cameron over at Wired, asked, in so many words, whether Nvidia had become too big to govern.

But he didn't use the words "too big to govern" or refer to a concept I've been calling "tech extensity." [1]

Instead, he quoted Edward Fishman, director of the Council on Foreign Relations' Maurice R. Greenberg Center for Geoeconomics, who said:

[s]ome tech companies have become so big—and so important to the stock market—that Washington is reluctant to hold them accountable for national security lapses.

In 'How Big Tech Becomes Ungovernable' I discussed how companies like Nvidia become so big, and society so dependent on their products (or in this case, their market impact), that they effectively become too big to govern. I also laid out the concept of "tech extensity," which is where something that has a great deal of breadth, scope, or reach (be it a person, company, or product), becomes deeply entrenched in a system. It's not about being the best—it's about becoming indispensable.

Henry Kissinger was an extensive force in geopolitics, diplomacy, and international relations. He was a fixture across administrations, and remained a power broker long after he left politics. That extensity and indispensability is probably what kept him from facing any consequences for policies that were arguably responsible for some very serious and devastating policies affecting millions between 1969 and 1976.

From the Kissinger example, I discussed how a handful of tech companies, and their multi-billionaire CEOs, have engineered "systems that are so intertwined and spread across so much of our lives" that they are essentially ungovernable, and how this is likely to get worse if/when ASI is realized.

Imagine a multi-trillion-dollar SpaceX, Google, Nvidia, Amazon, Meta, Oracle, or Microsoft—or more likely, a few of these firms—acting as quasi-national capitalist states, bolstered by super-intelligent AI systems, doing basically whatever they want, ungovernable by nation states that have all been captured. It's all well and good to have laws, but if a handful of corporations become effective states unto themselves, i.e., suppliers of the information, infrastructure, energy, technology, supply chains, and even the money, what even are laws at that point?

Well now, we have a modern-day Kissinger example. We're witnessing in real-time what happens when companies, and the CEOs who run them, are too big to govern: markets panic, the powerful intervene, and they get away with it.

FAFO, but without finding out

On November 8, Huang admitted to an extramarital affair with a direct report, against a backdrop of questions about a connection to Chinese intelligence. On November 12, he resigned. By then, Nvidia's board, the DOJ and Commerce Departments, the SEC, the State Department, Congress, and the California AG all had open inquiries — into national security risks, chip smuggling, and whether Huang had misled the public. The infidelity was never the point. It was a proxy for judgment and risk.

Then the market panicked:

  • The Nasdaq Composite fell from 25,253 on Nov. 9 to 22,618 on Nov. 20, down 10.4%.
  • The S&P 500 fell 8.5% over the same stretch; the Dow, 8.1%.
  • Nvidia's own share price dropped from roughly $216 to $126.

Some of that slide had independent causes; markets rarely move on one story. But Huang's reinstatement is harder to explain away.

Donald Trump declared that Huang "did nothing wrong" and leaned on the board to bring him back before any investigations were completed. On November 23, they did, and the Nasdaq jumped 6.5% and the S&P 4.7%—both their best single days since April 2025. The next day, Trump said a pardon was on the table, which is a curious thing to offer someone who did nothing wrong.

By my view, nothing about the underlying risk changed, at least based on public-facing materials. What changed was that everyone involved got a clear look at the price of accountability, and they decided to look the other way. Or, as the Zvi summarized on Substack: "We like money. Jensen Huang makes us money."

In short, if markets literally crash because you're a "generational CEO" and society has become so dependent on the products and circular economy you've helped to create that the President of the United States rallies to your defense, that makes you indispensable, and probably too big to govern.

Huang, quite literally, demonstrated that for those with extensive reach, you can do plenty of "fucking around", and not have to worry about any of the messiness of "finding out."

What actually matters

I'm reminded of Trump's infamous statement on the campaign trail in 2016:

I could stand in the middle of Fifth Avenue and shoot somebody, and I wouldn't lose any voters, OK? It's, like, incredible.

That's the problem with extensity and the erosion of friction[2] that comes from our growing dependency on Big Tech, the foundation model developers, and their leadership. The incremental capitulations and the affordances we grant to these "generational CEOs" add up. At some point, they will realize (if they haven't already) that they're so vital to the economy, the AI race, and society, that they can figuratively or literally shoot somebody on Fifth Avenue and never have to "find out."

I've spent the last few months poring over the literature on extreme power concentration[3], gradual disempowerment[4], and AI-enabled stable authoritarianism[5], and this is the future I worry about the most. I get that power concentration itself isn't new, and wealthy, powerful people have managed to escape liability for millennia, but it really feels like the exceptionalism is escaping containment, moving from local, isolated examples of despotic kings and Russian oligarchs, towards global ungovernability.

If society keeps treating these men and their companies as special and unique talents and platforms who can't be sullied with things like consequences or rules, one day, they will actually become ungovernable.

I don't think this will be immediate, or even obvious. The CEOs of these companies are all smart, capable, and have more money and resources than any human in history. They know how to operate, and Huang, for his part, probably won't do anything egregious, at least in the short term. So the path won't be

Sex scandal → murderbots → global takeover → human annihilation

Rather, it'll be subtle and gradual, with each escalating step seeming as benign or overblown as the one before. That's certainly the mechanism that Kulveit et al. describe in Gradual Disempowerment: institutions don't lose control through a dramatic takeover, they lose leverage as the things they depend on stop needing them back.

I'm worried, as is often the case with human outrage, that our moral Overton Windows will shift subtly as the gravity of the escalations shift. And that we'll collectively use the same reasoning as many did in this case to justify those future acts.

But, if we don't react to these ethics canaries, we might also start seeing ever-incremental backsliding and "disempowerment spirals"[6] much of this aided by advanced models, including:

  • increased regulatory capture & political corruption
  • privatized mass-surveillance
  • unconstrained platform power[7] and path dependencies[8]
  • AI models with secret loyalties[9] acting on behalf of the developers, not society
  • revision of the social contract between governments and individuals[10]
  • information concentration, mis- and disinformation
  • unaccountable political and voter manipulation
  • middle-powers digital vassalage,[11] and weaponized interdependence[12]
  • the erosion of the rule of law, institutions, and fundamental rights.

I don't want to see that world. And I want more people to start paying attention before it's too late.[13]

Which leads to a testable prediction: the next time a CEO with comparable market weight faces credible allegations of serious misconduct, the consequences will be faster to evaporate and the justifications more openly economic. If instead we see a board or regulator hold the line against a market-moving executive, I'd count that as real evidence that extensity has limits, and I'd be glad to be wrong.
